notes.meaning: The two angels who had visited Abraham arrived at Sodom in the evening. Lot was sitting at the city gate, which was the public square where town leaders and judges gathered to conduct business. When he saw the visitors, he stood up, showed them honor, and bowed low to welcome them.

Lot urged the travelers to come into his house, wash their feet, and spend the night safely. The visitors at first replied that they would stay in the open town square. In that region, travelers often slept outdoors, but Lot knew the grave danger of Sodom's streets at night.

Lot pleaded with the men so urgently that they finally agreed to come inside his home. He prepared a feast for them and baked flatbread without yeast so it could be served quickly. His strong persistence showed how eager he was to protect these strangers from the townspeople.

Before the guests could go to sleep, the men of Sodom surrounded Lot's house. Men of every age, from young boys to old men, joined the crowd from every part of the city. This showed that the whole town was corrupt and that no righteous people were left to stand up for what was good.

The mob called out to Lot and demanded that he send his visitors out so they could abuse them sexually. Their words revealed the shameless violence and depravity of the city. Instead of offering customary hospitality to strangers, the citizens sought to harm them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters hold that the primary sin of Sodom in this passage was violent inhospitality and cruelty toward strangers rather than sexual sin.

notes.meaning: Lot stepped outside the house to speak directly to the crowd, carefully shutting the door behind him. He did this to shield his guests from view and prevent the mob from rushing inside. He hoped to calm their anger by speaking with them face-to-face.

Lot pleaded with his neighbors not to commit such a wicked act, addressing them politely as brothers. He used friendly language to try to soften their fury and awaken their conscience. Even in a frightening moment, he tried to restrain their evil desires.

In extreme desperation, Lot offered his two unmarried daughters to the mob instead of the visitors. In the ancient world, hosts felt an absolute duty to protect anyone under their roof. Even so, commentators agree that offering his own daughters was a terrible and inexcusable moral failure.

The crowd angrily told Lot to step aside and ridiculed him for acting like a judge over them. Since Lot was an outsider who had moved there, they deeply resented his moral correction. They threatened to treat him worse than his guests and moved forward to break down the door.

The two visitors inside reached out, pulled Lot back into the safety of the house, and shut the door. God did not abandon his servant to the fury of the crowd. Divine help stepped in at the very moment human strength had failed.

The angels struck the men outside, both young and old, with sudden blindness and confusion of sight. Unable to see clearly, the attackers wore themselves out groping around trying to find the doorway. This miracle stopped their violent assault and proved that divine judgment had arrived.

The visitors asked Lot whether he had any other family members in Sodom, such as sons, daughters, or sons-in-law. They told him to gather everyone who belonged to him and get them out of the city immediately. God showed extraordinary mercy by offering rescue to Lot's entire household.

The angels explained that they were sent by the Lord to destroy the entire city. The outcry against the people's terrible wickedness had grown so loud before God that judgment could no longer wait. The holy angels serve as ministers of God's justice as well as his mercy.

Lot hurried into the night to warn the men who were pledged to marry his daughters, telling them the Lord was about to ruin the city. His future sons-in-law thought he was only joking and refused to take him seriously. Lot's worldly compromises had weakened his spiritual credibility so much that his family ignored his warning.

At daybreak, the angels urged Lot to hurry, telling him to take his wife and the two daughters still at home. If they delayed any longer, they would be swept away in the city's punishment. The time for discussion was over because the destruction was close at hand.

Lot still hesitated, lingering because it was painful to leave his home and possessions behind. Because of the Lord's great compassion, the angels grabbed the hands of Lot, his wife, and his daughters and pulled them safely outside the walls. They were delivered not by their own promptness, but entirely by God's mercy.

Once they were outside, the angel commanded them to run for their lives toward the mountains without stopping or looking back. Looking behind would show a longing heart for the sinful place God had condemned. True rescue required leaving Sodom completely behind in both body and mind.

Lot pleaded with the Lord's messenger, begging that he might not have to go all the way to the mountains. Even after being pulled from danger, his faith was weak and he struggled to obey fully. He wanted to negotiate his own place of safety instead of following God's clear directions.

Lot recognized that the Lord had shown him extraordinary kindness by saving his life. Yet he was afraid the mountain was too far away and that the disaster would catch up with him and kill him. His fear led him to doubt God's power to protect him on the journey.

Lot pointed to a small nearby town and asked permission to escape there instead. He argued that because it was only a small village, sparing it would be a little matter. He hoped he could find safety there while avoiding the hard climb into the hills.

The Lord kindly granted Lot's request and promised not to destroy that town. God showed remarkable patience with Lot's weak faith and fears. This answered plea reveals how gently God treats his frail servants when they call out to him.

The angel urged Lot to run there quickly because judgment could not fall until he had reached safety. God's righteous wrath was held back until his servant was out of harm's way. Because Lot had called the place small, the town was given the name Zoar, which means little.

The sun was rising across the land just as Lot entered the safety of Zoar. The peaceful dawn gave no natural sign of the sudden catastrophe about to strike the valley. God's timing brought deliverance to his servant before judgment fell on the wicked.

The Lord rained burning sulfur and fire down upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the heavens. This fiery storm was a direct, supernatural act of divine justice against unrepentant sin. The text emphasizes that the judgment came straight from God above.

God wiped out those cities, the whole valley plain, all the inhabitants, and everything growing out of the ground. The lush, fertile land was turned into an empty wasteland. What had once looked as beautiful as the garden of Eden became a lasting picture of divine judgment.

Lot's wife walked behind him and looked back longingly toward the city, disobeying the angel's clear command. Because her heart was still tied to Sodom's lifestyle and wealth, judgment overtook her, and she became a pillar of salt. Jesus later pointed to her as a solemn warning against turning back to a sinful world.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many commentators suggest she lingered behind, was suffocated by the fiery sulfur fumes, and became encrusted in the thick mineral salt common around the Dead Sea.

notes.meaning: Early the next morning, Abraham went back to the place near Hebron where he had stood in prayer before the Lord. He wanted to see what had happened to the valley cities he had interceded for. His early return showed his deep concern and watchful faith.

Looking down toward the plain of Sodom and Gomorrah, Abraham saw thick smoke rising like smoke from a giant furnace. The entire region was covered in black smoke and ruin. The terrible sight proved that the cities had been completely overthrown just as God had warned.

When God destroyed the cities of the valley, he remembered Abraham and brought Lot safely out of the disaster. Lot was rescued not because of his own spiritual strength, but because God honored Abraham's faithful prayers. God is faithful to answer the prayers of his people.

Lot eventually felt too frightened to stay in Zoar, so he moved up into the limestone mountains with his two daughters. They took shelter inside a mountain cave. After losing all his herds, home, and wealth, Lot ended his days in isolation and poverty.

The older daughter told the younger that their father was getting old and that there were no men left in the land to marry them. Having seen the destruction of the plain, they mistakenly believed the whole world was ruined and their family line would end. Their dark perspective showed how deeply Sodom's corrupt culture had shaped their thinking.

The older sister proposed that they get their father drunk with wine so they could sleep with him and have children. Although Lot had fled the city of Sodom, the morals of Sodom still lived in his daughters. They chose to commit a shameful sin instead of trusting God for their future.

That night they gave their father wine until he was heavily intoxicated, and the older daughter went in and lay with him. Lot was so drunk that he was completely unaware of when she lay down or when she left. His lack of self-control stripped away his moral judgment and led him into deep disgrace.

The following day, the older daughter told the younger that the plan had worked and urged her to do the same thing that night. She suggested making their father drunk again so the younger sister could also become pregnant. Sin was repeated without any shame or regret.

They made Lot drunk with wine again that second night, and the younger daughter went in and slept with him while he remained unaware. Lot's repeated drunkenness showed how quickly one careless choice opens the door to another. Both sisters completed their sinful scheme in the darkness of the cave.

As a result of their scheme, both of Lot's daughters became pregnant by their own father. The man who had stood against the wicked mob in Sodom fell into shocking dishonor alone in a cave. This sad outcome shows that even those rescued by God's mercy can fall into ruin when they let down their guard.

The older daughter gave birth to a son and named him Moab, a name related to the phrase meaning from the father. Instead of hiding the act, the name openly declared the child's incestuous origin. He became the ancestor of the Moabite nation, which later became a frequent enemy of Israel.

The younger daughter also gave birth to a son and named him Ben-ammi, which means son of my people or son of my kin. He became the ancestor of the Ammonite nation, who also became long-standing rivals of Israel. The tragic end of Lot's family warns that compromising with worldly ways leaves lasting scars for generations.
